title: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files
titleZh: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files
author: shmulc
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。

comments.author: bcherny
comments.textRawHtml:
Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.

That said, a few thoughts:

1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)

2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.

3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see https://github.com/security/plans)

children.author: syllogism
children.textRawHtml:
I want to draw deterministic boundaries around what the agent can do. I don't want a probabilistic approach to security.

My view is that if the agent can decide to do something, nothing stops that thing from being done accidentally, and any attacker that can inject text into its context can do that thing.

children.author: uw_rob
children.textRawHtml: Deterministic boundaries appear to be best solved with sandboxes/microVMs/remote infra and unique identities with probabilistic guardrails on top. The old deterministic allow/deny list running on bare metal didn't meaningfully solve the problem of giving Claude determinism. Humans got approval fatigue, and eventually, Claude got access to something like 'python3 FILE.py' and Claude could go to the races by updating 'FILE.py'.

children.author: syllogism
children.textRawHtml:
The allow/deny list functionality was trash though. If I have a once-off workflow and I want to execute Claude within it, I can't even give it a whitelist of allowed tools.

I definitely prefer auto-mode to the granularity of prompts I was getting from Claude. But I also want to be able to use deterministic rules, and Claude Code's functionality for it sucks.

children.textRawHtml: They aren't. Allowlists are a deterministic tool. That's the whole point: instructing an llm to review itself is nondeterministic, and thus not a good tool for permissions, compared to allowlists, which are.

children.author: socalgal2
children.textRawHtml: In my experience, Allowlists are not deterministic because the #1 thing the LLM does is write python scripts nearly every prompt and ask permission to execute its latest script. I know of no developers who review that code since it would make the process too slow to be useful. So YOLO! Yes, Claude/Codex/Gemini, you can execute the python you just wrote, even though I didn't review it and you have access to the entire machine and so every command I didn't give permission to execute you could just have written the equivalent python.

children.author: futhey
children.textRawHtml:
I'm not here to be critical, but the hoops you have to jump through to get Claude out of .env is more than it should be. You basically need an agent to write it if it's anything complicated, like, allow .env.example but not .env.*.

Whereas that should probably be default on instead, and this should apply to other known sensitive folders. A simpler system like .agentignore would be even better.

I like auto mode but "the agent supervises itself" is a bad compliance/safety answer on its own.

children.author: kstenerud
children.textRawHtml:
This is EXACTLY why I never use an agent outside of https://github.com/kstenerud/yoloai

I appreciate that you're trying to make Claude Code safer, but the agent really needs to be a lot more restricted in its reach rather than its actions.

The agent should NOT have ANY access to:

- Your ENV

- Your homedir

- The network at large

- ANY other directory on your system

- No, not even your workdir.

The only safe way to use an agent is COMPLETELY isolated by a container or VM, using git semantics to extract its output.
